newsitem.title: USA: Heinz seeking global growth in pet food business.
newsitem.headline: Heinz seeking global growth in pet food business.

text.p: H.J. Heinz Co. -- a name that brings ketchup to the minds of most consumers -- is aggressively expanding its second-largest business unit, pet food, a global market in which the battle for market share is raging, company officials say.

"In soup, Campbell's won the war in the U.S. In baby food, Gerber won in the U.S., and that's fine with us," said Heinz President William Johnson. "Pet food is one of the few categories around the world where the war is not over. Pet food around the world is a battle that will continue to rage over the next few years."

Once a faltering unit that faced an uncertain future, Heinz Pet Products generates more than $1 billion in sales, more than 10 percent of the company's total revenues. It is the Pittsburgh-based company's second-largest business segment behind food service.
Heinz Pet Products manufactures some of the best-known cat and dog foods and snacks, including 9 Lives, Kibbles 'n Bits, Meaty Bone and Gravy Train.

During the past decade, H.J. Heinz made a string of pet food acquisitions, boosting the segment's global presence. Company officials said more such acquisitions were likely and that Heinz Pet Products could enter joint ventures in Europe.

The pet food market is highly competitive, but Johnson said the growth potential was enormous because a growing number of people were getting pets and want a high standard of living for their furry friends.
"Pet food is a real opportunity," he said. "It's a $20 (billion) to $25 billion business worldwide."

Heinz Pet Products is striving for "global leadership" but that doesn't necessarily mean becoming the biggest, Johnson said. "Our goal is to be the highest quality, most consistently profitable, most innovative pet food company, and continue to provide the profit growth and margin structure we've provided."

Privately held Mars is the world's largest pet food producer, generating more than $4 billion in sales. Ralston Purina Co. of St. Louis is the largest U.S. producer with Nestle SA of Switzerland and Heinz "neck and neck" in the No. 2 slot, said Heinz Pet Products President Mike Milone.
Heinz Pet Products has 17 percent to 18 percent of the U.S. market and 5 percent to 6 percent of the world market, he said.
Milone said the unit could capture 10 percent of the world market by making a push into some of the fastest-growing regions, including Latin America and Asia.
He also said there is room for growth in the U.S. market, which is growing 4 percent to 5 percent annually in dollar terms of dollars.
"There are some real opportunities ... We're looking everywhere," he said.

While declining to be specific, Milone said Heinz Pet Products was seeking acquisition opportunities and working on several product and packaging innovations. He said the unit also could sell pet supplies, such as toys and food dishes.
"It would be very difficult for us (to be the world's largest) without significant acquisitions," Milone said. "Instead, we want to be the company that consumers, competitors and retailers watch."

The business at one time faced an uncertain future. Johnson began his Heinz career 15 years ago by running the business, which at that time was based in California and posting about $350 million in sales.

Johnson moved the business to its current home of Cincinnati and closed several plants and warehouses, slashing costs. The unit also began what Johnson called "price-based costing," selling multiple cans of pet food for a small sum such as one dollar, and increased its line of pet snacks.
"We got the costs out and the volume and margins up," Johnson said. "What we want to do in the future is take our expertise and go into emerging markets ... China, India, Latin America."
